data.text/html:
Gaussian Processes: distributions over functions

An interactive companion to DataMListic's video "Gaussian Processes". A Gaussian process (GP) doesn't hand you one function that fits your data. It hands you a whole distribution of functions, and that distribution tells you where you can trust the fit and where you can't. In this notebook you'll build a GP from scratch in numpy, click data points into existing, and watch the uncertainty collapse around them.

data.text/markdown:
Color language (same everywhere in this notebook)

color meaning
red observed data points
green the GP mean ||(m(x)||) (prior or posterior)
blue band ||(\pm 2\sigma||) uncertainty (~95% region)
thin multi-colored lines individual sample functions drawn from the GP
Roadmap (follows the video): ① what a GP is → ② the prior → ③ the posterior (click to add data) → ④ kernels → ⑤ combining kernels → ⑥ a practical example → sandbox, quiz, recap.

1 · A GP is a distribution over functions

"A Gaussian process is a collection of random variables where any finite subset follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution."
We write ||[f(x) \sim \mathcal{GP}\big(m(x),\; k(x, x')\big)||]
  • ||(m(x)||) is the mean function: the expected value of ||(f||) at ||(x||) (usually ||(0||)).
  • ||(k(x,x')||) is the covariance function or kernel: how strongly ||(f(x)||) and ||(f(x')||) move together.
The video's trick: pick just five points ||(x_1,\dots,x_5||). A GP says their function values are jointly Gaussian, ||[\begin{bmatrix} f(x_1)\\ \vdots \\ f(x_5)\end{bmatrix} \sim \mathcal N\!\left(\mathbf 0,\; K\right),\qquad K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j).||]Sample that vector, connect the dots, and you have a (rough) function. Add more points and the dots become a smooth curve. It's like rolling a bunch of correlated dice together: neighbours tend to land on similar numbers.

At \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\ell=3||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e the whole matrix glows and samples barely bend.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eNotice that average |jump| shrinks as \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(n||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e grows: neighbours become more correlated, which is exactly what makes the function \u003cem\u003econtinuous\u003c/em\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
2 · The prior: functions before you see data

Before observing anything, we choose a prior. For simplicity the mean function is set to zero, ||(m(x)=0||) (the green line; red in the video). The kernel gives every point a variance ||(k(x,x)=\sigma^2||), so the blue band ||(0 \pm 2\sigma||) is the 95% region where the functions are expected to live. Every sample below is a full function drawn from ||(\mathcal{GP}(0, k_{\text{RBF}})||). The band is the same width everywhere: the prior has no reason to be more confident anywhere.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eRaise \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\sigma||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e: the band and the samples stretch vertically, but their \u003cem\u003ewiggliness\u003c/em\u003e doesn't change. \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\sigma||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e is \"how far\", \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\ell||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e is \"how fast\".\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eShrink \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\ell||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e to 0.3 and compare: same band, very different functions. The band alone can't tell you the kernel; the samples can.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eCheck the readout: ~95% of all sampled values land inside the blue band, whatever you choose.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
3 · The posterior: click data into existence

When we observe data, the distribution updates. Conditioning a Gaussian on some of its coordinates gives another Gaussian, so the posterior at test points ||(X_*||) given data ||((X, \mathbf y)||) with noise ||(\sigma_n||) is ||[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf m_* &= K_*^\top\,(K + \sigma_n^2 I)^{-1}\,\mathbf y \\ \Sigma_* &= K_{**} - K_*^\top\,(K + \sigma_n^2 I)^{-1}\,K_* \end{aligned} ||]with ||(K = k(X,X)||), ||(K_* = k(X,X_*)||), ||(K_{**} = k(X_*,X_*)||). The first line pulls the green mean through the red points; the second line subtracts uncertainty wherever the kernel says "this test point is correlated with an observation". Click anywhere in the plot to add an observation. Drag points to move them; double-click one to delete it. The widget solves the GP (Cholesky, in JavaScript) on every frame, so you see the update instantly.

Add \u003cstrong\u003eone\u003c/strong\u003e point: the mean jumps through it and the band pinches to ~σₙ there, but only within about \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\ell||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e of it.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eAdd points one by one from left to right, like the video: \"uncertainty is smallest near our data points and grows larger as we move away\". Grow it to 3: one point informs the whole axis.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4 · Kernels decide what functions you can represent

"Basically the kernel determines what kinds of functions we can represent."
The video walks through three kernels:
kernel formula samples look like
RBF (squared exponential) ||(k(x,x') = \sigma^2 \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\lvert x-x'\rvert^2}{2\ell^2}\right)||) smooth, gradually varying
Periodic ||(k(x,x') = \sigma^2 \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{2\sin^2(\pi \lvert x-x'\rvert / p)}{\ell^2}\right)||) repeating with period ||(p||)
Linear ||(k(x,x') = \sigma_b^2 + \sigma^2 (x-c)(x'-c)||) straight lines, random slope & intercept
Left chart: one row of the kernel, ||(k(0, x')||): how much ||(f(0)||) is correlated with ||(f(x')||). Middle: the full covariance matrix. Right: prior samples. Read them together: the shape of the kernel row is the personality of the functions.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePeriodic\u003c/strong\u003e, \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(p=2.5||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e: the kernel row comes back to its peak at \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(x'=2.5, 5||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e. The covariance matrix shows stripes, and the readout \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(k(0,p)/k(0,0)||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e would be exactly 1: points one period apart are \u003cem\u003eperfectly\u003c/em\u003e correlated.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLinear\u003c/strong\u003e: the row is a straight line and the band is a bow-tie (narrowest at \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(x=c||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e). Move \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(c||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e and the pinch point follows. This kernel is \u003cem\u003enot stationary\u003c/em\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eRBF\u003c/strong\u003e: shrink \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\ell||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e and watch the row narrow, the matrix's bright diagonal thin out and the samples get busier. Same story as Section 1.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
5 · Combining kernels: add and multiply

"The really interesting thing about kernels is that we can combine them to create complex patterns."
Sums and products of valid kernels are valid kernels: ||[k_{+}(x,x') = k_{\text{per}}(x,x') + k_{\text{lin}}(x,x') \qquad k_{\times}(x,x') = k_{\text{per}}(x,x')\cdot k_{\text{lin}}(x,x')||]
  • Sum = independent functions added: a linear trend with periodic fluctuations riding on top ("a steadily growing economy with seasonal fluctuations").
  • Product = one modulates the other: the amplitude of the oscillations grows as we move away from the center.
The animation below morphs continuously through samples of the chosen GP. Every frame is an exact draw (the trick: ||(f(t) = L\,(z_1\cos t + z_2\sin t)||) with ||(z_1,z_2\sim\mathcal N(0,I)||) is again ||(\mathcal N(0, LL^\top)||)), so watch the family of shapes, not one curve.

The σ(x) chart shows the bow-tie.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eRBF × Periodic\u003c/strong\u003e is the \"locally periodic\" kernel: a repeating pattern that slowly changes its shape. Compare it with RBF + Periodic, where the pattern is fixed and a smooth wander is added.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
6 · Practical example: which kernel fits?

The video's finale: noisy data from an unknown pattern (the dashed true function, which in real life we would not know) and three GPs fit to the same red points:
  • RBF: "not bad, but it misses the main pattern, which is the oscillations".
  • Periodic: "captures the periodicity but doesn't capture the linear pattern".
  • Periodic + Linear: "captures the underlying pattern beautifully, with reasonable uncertainty estimates everywhere".
Here the true function is ||(f(x) = 0.3x + \sin(2\pi x / 2.5)||). Data are observed only on ||([-5, 2]||), so the region ||(x>2||) is a genuine extrapolation test. We score each kernel with the log marginal likelihood ||(\log p(\mathbf y\mid X)||) (how well the kernel explains the data, the quantity you'd maximise to tune hyperparameters) and with the RMSE against the truth on held-out ||(x||).

data.text/html: Highest log marginal likelihood: Periodic + Linear. Dashed vertical line = edge of the data; dashed olive = the true function.

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eLook right of the dashed line: RBF's mean drifts back to 0 and its band balloons, Periodic keeps waving but around the wrong level, Periodic + Linear keeps climbing with the trend.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eDrop to 5 observations: every model is uncertain, and the likelihood ranking can flip. With little data, the prior (the kernel) is doing most of the work.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eCrank the noise to 1.0: the GP means get smoother and the bands wider. The \u003cem\u003estructure\u003c/em\u003e the kernel assumes matters even more when the data are noisy.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
🧪 Sandbox

A second canvas with everything unlocked: pick any kernel (including periodic+linear and rbf+linear), set its hyperparameters, and click your own data. Below it, numpy re-fits the same data with every kernel and ranks them by log marginal likelihood. Challenges
  • Draw a rising zig-zag and find a kernel + settings that extrapolates it convincingly to the right.
  • Make the RBF's log marginal likelihood beat periodic+linear on data you drew.
  • Find settings where 2 posterior samples look completely different between the data points but identical at them.

Recap

concept the one-liner formula where you touched it
Gaussian process a distribution over functions; any finite set of values is jointly Gaussian ||(f \sim \mathcal{GP}(m, k)||) §1 correlated dice
Prior before data: mean 0, constant ±2σ band ||(f(X)\sim\mathcal N(0, K)||) §2 prior samples
Posterior condition on data: mean passes through points, uncertainty shrinks near them ||(m_*=K_*^\top(K+\sigma_n^2I)^{-1}y||), ||(\Sigma_*=K_{**}-K_*^\top(K+\sigma_n^2I)^{-1}K_*||) §3 click-to-add canvas
Kernels the kernel is the assumption: smooth (RBF), repeating (periodic), trend (linear) see §4 table §4 kernel explorer
Combining sums add behaviours, products modulate them ||(k_{per}+k_{lin}||), ||(k_{per}\cdot k_{lin}||) §5 animator
Model choice the right structure extrapolates; the log marginal likelihood helps pick it ||(\log p(y\mid X)||) §6 + sandbox
When to reach for a GP: regression with limited data, or whenever you need explicit uncertainty estimates (e.g. Bayesian optimization, the video's suggested next topic). Exact GPs cost ||(O(n^3)||), so beyond a few thousand points you need approximations.
